title: Tunable Mpemba Effect In A Prethermal Many-Body Spin Network
authors: Chaitali Shah, Cooper M. Selco, Leo Joon Il Moon, Ashok Ajoy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relaxation in an interacting system is determined not only by its initial distance from equilibrium, but also by the relaxation modes populated by the initial state. Here we experimentally observe and control the Mpemba effect, in which a state farther from equilibrium overtakes one initially closer, in an extended, disordered [MATH]C nuclear-spin network in diamond. Field cycling allows us to prepare distinct spatial polarization profiles by independently controlling hyperpolarization and defect-mediated relaxation. We then track their evolution under Floquet driving, which stabilizes a long-lived prethermal regime. We observe reproducible Mpemba crossings and tune the crossing time over several orders of magnitude, from late-time thermalization into the prethermal plateau. Semiclassical simulations show that randomly positioned paramagnetic defects create fast-relaxing regions and defect-poor regions that support the slowest collective relaxation mode. The Mpemba crossings are set by the initial state overlap with this mode. Our results demonstrate anomalous relaxation within a prethermal many-body regime and identify disorder, transport, and mode-selective state preparation as resources for controlling relaxation in extended spin networks.
tldr: Experimental observation and control of the Mpemba effect in a prethermal many-body spin network, demonstrating anomalous relaxation tunable over orders of magnitude.
motivation: Understanding how initial state preparation and disorder can control relaxation in interacting quantum systems, specifically the counterintuitive Mpemba effect where a farther-from-equilibrium state relaxes faster.
method: Field cycling in a diamond nuclear-spin network to prepare distinct polarization profiles, followed by Floquet driving to stabilize a prethermal regime; semiclassical simulations model defect-mediated relaxation.
result: Reproducible Mpemba crossings observed, with crossing time tunable over several orders of magnitude; crossings arise from initial state overlap with the slowest collective relaxation mode supported by defect-poor regions.
conclusion: Disorder, transport, and mode-selective state preparation are resources for controlling relaxation in extended spin networks, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Frame-Dependent Traces And The Third-Particle Paradox
authors: Luca Apadula Alessandro Palumbo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Paradox of the Third Particle arises when comparing subsystem descriptions across Quantum Reference Frame (QRF) perspectives. We isolate two distinct origins of the Paradox: the QRF covariance of the partial trace and the failure of the physical Hilbert space to inherit the kinematical tensor-product structure. We give an explicit counterexample to the Relational Trace (RT) resolution: an uncorrelated product state for which the RT statistical condition trivialises. We then introduce a new statistical consistency condition comparing subsystem discarding between external and internal QRFs, together with an associated frame-dependent map, the Perspective Relational Trace (PRT). We argue that our condition captures the operational content of the Paradox: rather than imposing consistency on the whole state space, we characterise exactly the states on which it holds in the Perspective-Neutral (PN) and Quantum-Information (QI) approaches. This separates three levels of description: a PN subsystem of a PN whole, where consistency fails on a characterised set that includes product states; a QI subsystem of a QI whole, where it holds for all states; and a QI subsystem obtained from a PN whole by kinematical partial trace, where the full weakly invariant algebra is recovered, yet consistency holds only on a proper subset. These results show that the PN approach can consistently describe only a closed, isolated system, while the QI approach can accommodate arbitrary subsystems. Tracing out a subsystem from a globally PN state yields a charge-superselected algebra, reproducing in a minimal QRF model the boundary-charge structure of edge modes. We understand the Paradox not as a genuine contradiction, but as the consequence of comparing inequivalent physical layers without tracking which information is externally and which internally accessible.
tldr: The paper resolves the Third-Particle Paradox in Quantum Reference Frames by distinguishing two origins and introducing a frame-dependent partial trace that clarifies when subsystem descriptions are consistent.
motivation: The Third-Particle Paradox challenges the consistency of subsystem descriptions across different quantum reference frames, which is fundamental to quantum information and relational quantum mechanics.
method: The authors analyze the paradox by separating QRF covariance issues from Hilbert space structure failures, propose a new statistical consistency condition, and define the Perspective Relational Trace (PRT) map.
result: They show that the Perspective-Neutral approach only works for closed systems, while the Quantum-Information approach handles arbitrary subsystems; tracing out from a PN state yields charge-superselected algebras akin to edge modes.
conclusion: The paradox is not a contradiction but a consequence of comparing inequivalent physical layers; the PRT provides a consistent operational framework for subsystem discarding across QRFs.

title: Mixed-state Topological Order And Error-correction Thresholds In non-Abelian Codes: Rigorous Results
authors: Max Mcginley Sun Woo P. Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a versatile and mathematically rigorous technique for bounding recovery thresholds in topological codes subject to noise. Our method captures the effect of applying an arbitrary (possibly non-Pauli) local noise channel to the code state of a broad class of two-dimensional codes, including surface codes, non-Abelian quantum doubles, and string-net codes. In each case, we prove that for noise strengths up to some explicit constant value, any initially encoded logical information can be recovered to high precision, and that the noise-corrupted state exhibits key hallmarks of mixed-state topological order: long-range entanglement and emergent higher-form symmetries. We also describe how these methods can be adapted to higher dimensions and correlated noise models.
tldr: Rigorous bounds on error-correction thresholds for non-Abelian topological codes under general local noise, demonstrating mixed-state topological order.
motivation: Understanding error thresholds in topological codes is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, especially for non-Abelian codes where rigorous results are scarce.
method: Develops a versatile mathematical technique using recovery maps and properties of mixed-state topological order to bound recovery thresholds for a broad class of 2D codes.
result: Proves explicit constant noise thresholds for surface codes, non-Abelian quantum doubles, and string-net codes, and shows that noise-corrupted states retain long-range entanglement and higher-form symmetries.
conclusion: The method provides rigorous guarantees for error correction in topological codes and can be extended to higher dimensions and correlated noise.

title: Tunable Nonlinear Electromechanics At The Zero-point Motion Scale
authors: Christoffer B. M{\o}ller, Roger Tormo-Queralt, Elsa V\'azquez-Rodr\'iguez, Victor Rom\'an-Rodr\'iguez, Marta Cagetti, Eneko Mateos-Madinabeitia, Janine C. Franz, Stefan Forstner, Sergio L. de Bonis, Luca Ornago, Maria El Abbassi, Seoho Jung, Andrew N. Cleland, David A. Czaplewski, Fabio Pistolesi, Adrian Bachtold
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinearity at the scale of zero-point motion opens new possibilities for the control and readout of nanomechanical systems, but achieving this remains a formidable challenge. Here we demonstrate that ultrastrong coupling (USC) between a nanotube mechanical oscillator and a double-quantum-dot electronic two-level system enables a mechanical Kerr (Duffing) nonlinearity at the zero-point motion scale. In the dispersive regime, this large coupling yields a mechanical anharmonicity of [MATH] - three orders of magnitude larger than in previous work - while preserving the predominantly mechanical nature of the lowest energy states. We further demonstrate a purely quadratic cavity-based continuous readout of the mechanical motion. This continuous nonlinear optomechanical readout is enforced by a double-quantum dot symmetry, which can be broken by gate tuning to introduce a large linear transduction. These results establish a tunable USC platform that enables strong mechanical anharmonicity and nonlinear continuous readout at the zero-point motion scale.
tldr: Demonstrates ultrastrong coupling between a nanotube mechanical oscillator and a double quantum dot, enabling a mechanical Kerr nonlinearity at the zero-point motion scale and a quadratic cavity readout.
motivation: Achieving nonlinearity at the zero-point motion scale is a formidable challenge that could enable new control and readout capabilities for nanomechanical systems.
method: The authors use a nanotube mechanical oscillator coupled ultrastrongly to a double-quantum-dot electronic two-level system, operating in the dispersive regime to realize a mechanical Kerr nonlinearity, and employ a quadratic cavity-based continuous readout enforced by double-quantum-dot symmetry.
result: They observe a mechanical anharmonicity three orders of magnitude larger than previous work, while preserving the mechanical nature of the lowest energy states, and demonstrate tunable linear transduction by breaking the symmetry.
conclusion: This establishes a tunable ultrastrong coupling platform that enables strong mechanical anharmonicity and nonlinear continuous readout at the zero-point motion scale, with potential applications in quantum sensing and transduction.

title: Spectral Gap Of The Davies Generator For The Mean-Field Heisenberg Model
authors: Joao Basso, Thiago Bergamaschi, Lin Lin, Michael Ragone, Kevin D. Stubbs
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mean-field Heisenberg ferromagnet is a quantum spin model on the complete graph with isotropic spin-1/2 interactions. This non-commuting Hamiltonian is permutation and [MATH] invariant, and its Gibbs states undergo an [MATH] symmetry breaking phase transition at inverse temperature [MATH]. We consider the associated Davies generator, a canonical model of open-system thermalization, and prove tight asymptotic estimates for its spectral gap at all noncritical temperatures. For fixed [MATH], the gap as a function of number of qubits [MATH] is [MATH], while for fixed [MATH] the gap is [MATH]. The matching upper bound of the spectral gap is witnessed by the total magnetization order parameter, suggesting that the low-temperature ([MATH]) slowdown is associated with broken continuous symmetry. Two key ingredients in our approach are a comparison argument, which introduces auxiliary generators to bound dissipation on nontrivial representations of the symmetry groups [MATH] and [MATH], and a decomposition of the space of observables into spherical tensor operators to reveal a form of monotonicity.
tldr: This paper proves tight asymptotic estimates for the spectral gap of the Davies generator for the mean-field Heisenberg model, revealing a slowdown at low temperatures due to broken continuous symmetry.
motivation: Understanding thermalization rates in quantum systems is fundamental to quantum thermodynamics; the spectral gap of the Davies generator controls the mixing time and thus the efficiency of thermal processes.
method: The authors use a comparison argument with auxiliary generators to bound dissipation on nontrivial representations of SU(2) and S_N, and decompose the space of observables into spherical tensor operators to reveal monotonicity.

conclusion: The spectral gap exhibits a phase transition at the critical temperature, with the low-temperature slowdown linked to the continuous symmetry breaking, providing rigorous bounds on thermalization times.

title: Quantum Advantage Of Nonlinear Quantum Battery And Superconducting Circuit Implementation
authors: Wei-Jun Han, Peng-Yu Sun, Guo-Feng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum battery is a novel energy storage device that operates on the principles of quantum mechanics. To enhance the charging performance of quantum batteries and further provide theoretical support for their physical implementation, we constructed an optical-field-dependent nonlinear quantum battery model. Meanwhile, we solved for the unbiased form of nonlinear interactions in this model, where the charging power of the proposed model exhibits a superlinear quantum advantage, and the charging time saturates the quantum speed limit. Through theoretical analysis, we confirm that this quantum advantage arises from the quantum effect of multiphoton absorption. Subsequently, with the derived nonlinear function form, we further investigated other properties of this nonlinear quantum battery. Finally, an experimental design scheme for this nonlinear quantum battery in superconducting quantum circuits is presented.
tldr: A nonlinear quantum battery model with optical-field-dependent interactions achieves superlinear charging power and saturates the quantum speed limit, with a superconducting circuit implementation proposed.
motivation: To enhance the charging performance of quantum batteries and provide theoretical support for their physical implementation.
method: Constructed an optical-field-dependent nonlinear quantum battery model, solved for the unbiased form of nonlinear interactions, and derived the charging power and time; then designed an experimental scheme using superconducting quantum circuits.
result: The model exhibits superlinear quantum advantage in charging power and saturates the quantum speed limit, attributed to multiphoton absorption.
conclusion: Nonlinear interactions can significantly improve quantum battery performance, and the proposed superconducting circuit design offers a feasible experimental platform.

title: Efficient Unclonable Encryption From Pauli Eigenstates
authors: Seyoon Ragavan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give, to our knowledge, the first plain-model, one-time information-theoretically secure, efficient unclonable encryption scheme for one classical bit. Previous work by Bhattacharyya and Culf (Nature Physics, 2026) and Bhattacharyya, Broadbent, and Culf either only showed [MATH] security loss or required inefficient encryption/decryption operations. We avoid both of these caveats; in doing so, we obtain (to our knowledge) the first plain-model construction of many-time secure [MATH] unclonable encryption for arbitrary polynomial-length messages, assuming the existence of pseudorandom function-like states (Bartusek and Goldin). The key is a uniformly random non-identity phase-free Pauli on [MATH] qubits, and bit [MATH] is encrypted as a random [MATH] eigenstate of that Pauli. The scheme is exponentially secure; we prove that the probability that both receivers recover the bit is at most [MATH] By a lower bound due to Broadbent, Culf, and Rochette, this is the best probability bound achievable with [MATH]-qubit ciphertexts (up to the constant hidden in the [MATH]). The main conceptual idea is to leverage, in a precise spectral sense, the balanced commutation-anticommutation structure of the Pauli group. The proof is intricate but completely elementary and makes use of standard spectral bound techniques. The main technical workhorse is a standalone linear-algebraic lemma that informally relates the positivity of two different operators, each capturing the intuition that if the two receivers can individually decrypt unusually often then they must also disagree often. tldr: First plain-model, information-theoretically secure unclonable encryption scheme for one classical bit using Pauli eigenstates, achieving optimal security bound.
motivation: Prior unclonable encryption schemes either had suboptimal security loss or required inefficient operations; this work aims to achieve both optimal security and efficiency in the plain model.
method: Encrypts a classical bit as a random eigenstate of a uniformly random non-identity phase-free Pauli on n qubits; security proof uses spectral bounds and a linear-algebraic lemma relating decryption success to disagreement probability.
result: Exponentially secure scheme with probability that both receivers recover the bit at most 2^{-n+1}, matching the lower bound up to a constant.
conclusion: Provides the first efficient, information-theoretically secure unclonable encryption in the plain model, with extensions to many-time security under pseudorandom function-like states.

title: Absent, Not Faint: Fisher-Information Limits And A Logarithmic Measurement-Design Cure For Passive Characterization Of Coherent Qubit Noise
authors: Yi Pan, Meng Hsiu Tsai, Weihang You, Hanqi Jiang, Junhao Chen, Wei Zhang, Isaac Lyngaas, Yingfeng Wang, Tianming Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibrating a quantum processor means estimating error parameters, and estimation theory usually assumes a parameter hard to estimate is faint: its signal is weak but present, so more repetitions or a richer model will recover it. This assumption fails for a leading hardware fault. A coherent over-rotation is a small systematic gate miscalibration. Measured through the cheapest data a device returns--one fixed-basis histogram--it is not faint but absent: to first order it leaves the distribution unchanged, indistinguishable from a compensating stochastic error, exactly as two numbers cannot be separated from their sum. For commuting single- and two-qubit transverse over-rotations, with known support on the canonical input, the histogram's Fisher information is singular along the fault's direction at zero angle, its Cramer-Rao bound is infinite, and no finite-variance, locally unbiased estimator recovers it. At a generic nonzero angle the degeneracy partly lifts; beyond four qubits it clears entirely, leaving conditioning, not absence, as the obstruction. The cure is a richer measurement, not a richer model: a fixed, logarithmically small set of extra settings makes every such fault visible. Visibility alone is not enough. The sampling cost is set by conditioning, not coverage, through a floor whose complete-family closed form is exponentially small in the qubit count. We prove the impossibility and cure, confirm both in exact simulation, show conditioning predicts recovery error across hundreds of designs, and observe a 3-5x bias gap on IBM Heron hardware as a consistency check. Non-commuting faults and unknown support remain open.
tldr: This paper identifies a fundamental limitation in passive qubit noise characterization—coherent over-rotations are invisible in fixed-basis histograms—and proposes a logarithmic measurement design to restore identifiability.
motivation: Calibrating quantum processors requires estimating error parameters, but coherent over-rotations (a common fault) are not faint but absent in standard measurements, making them impossible to estimate with finite variance.
method: The authors analyze the Fisher information matrix for commuting single- and two-qubit transverse over-rotations, prove the singularity at zero angle, and show that a logarithmically small set of extra measurement settings lifts the degeneracy.
result: They prove that no finite-variance locally unbiased estimator exists for zero-angle over-rotations, and demonstrate that conditioning (not coverage) determines recovery error, with a closed-form floor exponentially small in qubit count.
conclusion: A richer measurement design, not a richer model, cures the absence; non-commuting faults and unknown support remain open problems.

title: Inertial Asynchronous Computation
authors: Doruk Efe G\"okmen, Michel Fruchart, Dmitrii Zendrikov, Giacomo Indiveri, Giulio Biroli, Vincenzo Vitelli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computation is the controlled evolution of a state. Asynchronous evolutions, where all parts of the state change in their own time without stopping each other, put this control in jeopardy. It is in fact a mystery how natural processes perform asynchronous computations using many units with no global orchestration. Here we demonstrate how collective computational abilities can emerge in asynchronous many-body systems. The key insight is to split the physical "hardware" underlying the computation into two asymmetrically coupled parts, analogous to position and momentum in a harmonic oscillator. The resulting inertia nudges the evolution of the state so that the asynchronous computation proceeds in the right order. By treating our inertial asynchronous computer as a nonequilibrium material, we map out its phase diagram numerically and analytically using a framework we dub loop dynamical mean-field theory. We experimentally demonstrate our approach using analog spiking neuromorphic chips designed to mimic actual neurons in the brain. In addition, we construct software that can run on asynchronous hardware: we denoise movies whose clean versions were never seen during training, an instantiation of the generalization transition underlying modern machine learning. Our results point to a general strategy for reliable, decentralized computation in energy-constrained settings from dynamics self-assembly to cell differentiation.
tldr: This paper demonstrates how asynchronous computation can be reliably performed by introducing inertia via asymmetric coupling, treating the system as a nonequilibrium material and mapping its phase diagram.
motivation: Asynchronous evolutions in many-body systems risk losing control over computation; the mystery of how natural processes achieve reliable decentralized computation motivates this work.
method: The authors split the hardware into two asymmetrically coupled parts (analogous to position and momentum), use loop dynamical mean-field theory for analytical and numerical phase diagram mapping, and experimentally implement the approach on analog spiking neuromorphic chips.
result: They map out the phase diagram of the inertial asynchronous computer and demonstrate denoising of movies without clean training data, showing a generalization transition.
conclusion: The results point to a general strategy for reliable, decentralized computation in energy-constrained settings, relevant to dynamics self-assembly and cell differentiation.

title: Weak Permanent Anti-Concentration For Random Gaussian Matrices In Boson Sampling
authors: Fei Meng, Bin Cheng, Jianan Li, Man-Hong Yung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent demonstrations of quantum computational advantage have been driven largely by sampling problems. A prominent model, boson sampling, involves sampling from the output distribution of a linear optical network. However, its classical hardness hinges on two plausible yet less-studied conjectures: the average-case hardness of approximating Gaussian permanents, and the permanent anti-concentration conjecture (PACC). The PACC is a purely mathematical assertion regarding the distributional properties of random Gaussian matrices. While the typical magnitude of the permanent has been established for discrete random matrices, the complex Gaussian case, which governs transition amplitudes in linear optical networks, has remained open. Here, we establish a weak anti-concentration bound by upper-bounding the probability that a random Gaussian permanent is superexponentially smaller than its standard deviation. Tightening this bound to an inverse-polynomial fraction would prove the original PACC. As a corollary, we establish the typical magnitude of Gaussian permanents, on par with Tao and Vu's seminal result for Bernoulli matrices. Combined with the Aaronson-Arkhipov framework, our result implies that classically simulating boson sampling to within a superexponentially small total variation distance would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, assuming the remaining conjectures hold.
tldr: Establishes a weak anti-concentration bound for Gaussian permanents, supporting the hardness of boson sampling.
motivation: Boson sampling's classical hardness relies on the permanent anti-concentration conjecture (PACC), which was unproven for complex Gaussian matrices. Proving a weak version strengthens the theoretical foundation.
method: Uses probabilistic and combinatorial techniques to upper-bound the probability that a random Gaussian permanent is superexponentially smaller than its standard deviation.
result: Proves a weak anti-concentration bound and establishes the typical magnitude of Gaussian permanents, matching known results for Bernoulli matrices.
conclusion: The result implies that classically simulating boson sampling to within superexponentially small error collapses the polynomial hierarchy, assuming other conjectures hold.

title: Capacitive Loading In Two-dimensional Fluxonium Quantum Processors
authors: Quan Guan, Guo Xuan Chan, Xu Dou, Chunqing Deng, Lijing Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capacitive loading has emerged as a major obstacle to scaling fluxonium qubits from one-dimensional to highly connected two-dimensional (2D) architectures, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. We derive an analytical relation between the qubit capacitance budget and the achievable capacitive coupling to external circuit elements, identifying the parasitic capacitances of Josephson junctions and Josephson junction arrays as the dominant source of capacitive loading while showing that the qubit-pad geometry can instead be engineered to mitigate it. Building on these insights, we formulate practical design principles and numerically demonstrate ultrafast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates in 2D fluxonium architectures. Our results reveal that capacitive loading does not constitute a fundamental limit for 2D fluxonium quantum processors.
tldr: This paper identifies parasitic capacitances of Josephson junctions as the dominant source of capacitive loading in 2D fluxonium processors and provides design principles to mitigate it, enabling ultrafast high-fidelity two-qubit gates.
motivation: Capacitive loading limits scaling fluxonium qubits to 2D architectures, but its physical origin is poorly understood. Understanding and mitigating it is crucial for building large-scale fluxonium quantum processors.
method: The authors derive an analytical relation between qubit capacitance budget and achievable coupling, identify parasitic capacitances of Josephson junctions as the main source, and show that qubit-pad geometry can be engineered to reduce loading. They then numerically demonstrate two-qubit gates using these insights.
result: They show that capacitive loading is not a fundamental limit and demonstrate numerically ultrafast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates in 2D fluxonium architectures.
conclusion: The findings provide practical design principles for scaling fluxonium qubits to 2D architectures, overcoming a major obstacle in the field.

title: Electron Shuttling As A Probe For Charge Defects
authors: Hamza Jnane, Tamas Daniel Lipovics, Guido Burkard
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon spin qubits are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, but their performance is limited by charge noise, widely attributed to two-level fluctuators (TLFs). The location of individual TLFs is generally unknown, and existing methods to localise them does not scale favourably with device size. Here, we show that electron shuttling turns a single mobile spin into a scanning probe of individual defects. We show that by shuttling a spin over a range of distances and tracking its coherence loss, one can localise defects along the channel and constrain their switching rate and fluctuation amplitude. Because one shuttled electron sweeps an extended region, the approach scales more favourably than previous methods. Our protocol requires no additional hardware and provides a practical route to mapping the charge-defect landscape of large silicon devices, enabling defect-aware calibration and avoidance in shuttling-based architectures.
tldr: This paper proposes using electron shuttling to localize charge defects in silicon spin qubit devices, enabling scalable defect mapping.
motivation: Charge noise from two-level fluctuators limits silicon spin qubit performance, but existing defect localization methods do not scale with device size.
method: By shuttling a single electron spin over varying distances and measuring its coherence loss, the protocol infers defect positions, switching rates, and fluctuation amplitudes.
result: The approach scales favorably compared to previous methods, requiring no additional hardware and providing a practical route to map charge defects in large silicon devices.
conclusion: Electron shuttling can serve as a scanning probe for charge defects, enabling defect-aware calibration and avoidance in shuttling-based quantum computing architectures.

title: Molecular Chiral Discrimination Through Symmetry-breaking Spin Dynamics
authors: Tianyu Xie, Yucheng Hao, Mingzhe Liu, Mengqi Wang, Shaoyi Xu, Zhiyuan Zhao, Chang-Kui Duan, Ya Wang, Fazhan Shi, Jiangfeng Du
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular chirality plays a crucial role in physics, chemistry, life sciences and pharmacology. Nowadays, the chiral discrimination and control at the single-molecule level is urgently needed to reveal the origin of the chirality-relevant phenomena by recovering the information disturbed by the ensemble averaging. The method of magnetic resonance (MR), as one of powerful tools for structure analysis, is blind to the molecular chirality in the absence of a chiral reagent. Here we propose and experimentally demonstrate a direct MR-based method for determining the chirality at the single-molecule level through constructing the symmetry-breaking dynamics of nearby nuclear spins. In principle, the mirror asymmetry of two enantiomers in real space is manifested by breaking the joint symmetry of the mirror reflection and time reversal in spin space under spin dynamics. Experimentally, two enantiomers are indistinguishable from the dynamics of strongly-coupled but unpolarized nuclear spins, but diverge evidently in the dynamical results that break the field-inversion symmetry after spins are polarized. Our method and results will benefit the study of chirality-induced properties in the fields of chemistry and biology.
tldr: A magnetic resonance method for single-molecule chiral discrimination via symmetry-breaking spin dynamics in nearby nuclear spins.
motivation: Molecular chirality is crucial in many fields, but existing methods lack single-molecule sensitivity. Magnetic resonance is blind to chirality without chiral reagents, so a direct MR-based method is needed.
method: The authors construct symmetry-breaking dynamics of nearby nuclear spins to manifest mirror asymmetry of enantiomers, breaking the joint symmetry of mirror reflection and time reversal in spin space. Experiments use polarized nuclear spins to observe divergence in dynamics.
result: Two enantiomers are indistinguishable from dynamics of unpolarized spins but diverge clearly when spins are polarized, enabling direct chirality determination at the single-molecule level.
conclusion: The method provides a direct MR-based approach for chiral discrimination at the single-molecule level, benefiting studies of chirality-induced properties in chemistry and biology.

title: Maximal Fisher Budget Forces Blind Directions In Bipartite Collective SU(d) Metrology
authors: Tariq Aziz, Naeem Akhtar, Dong Wang, Augusto Smerzi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For pure two-qudit probes used in a single fixed setting to estimate a common SU(d) transformation, maximal total Fisher sensitivity and full local identifiability are mutually exclusive. We derive exact identities that determine the trace of the quantum Fisher information matrix from two measurable probe properties: exchange symmetry and collective polarization. Every maximizer is exchange symmetric and maximally entangled. Its Fisher matrix has equal sensitivity in every visible direction, while [MATH] generator directions are blind. More generally, weak compatibility, defined by vanishing mean generator commutators, forces at least [MATH] blind directions for every pure bipartite probe. A probe-defined antiunitary invariant classifies the complete Fisher spectrum at maximal entanglement, and approaches to the optimum that preserve exchange symmetry have a divergent Holevo cost. The bipartite obstruction is sharp in particle number: for [MATH], generalized GHZ probes can satisfy weak compatibility, attain the corresponding [MATH]-partite Fisher trace bound, and retain full local identifiability. Hence, Fisher sensitivity, weak compatibility, identifiability, and attainable precision are distinct resources in quantum metrology with noncommuting generators.
tldr: This paper proves that maximal Fisher sensitivity and full local identifiability are mutually exclusive for pure two-qudit probes estimating a common SU(d) transformation, identifying a fundamental trade-off in quantum metrology.
motivation: Quantum metrology with noncommuting generators faces fundamental limits; understanding the interplay between Fisher information, identifiability, and entanglement is crucial for optimal sensing.
method: The authors derive exact identities for the trace of the quantum Fisher information matrix in terms of exchange symmetry and collective polarization, and use an antiunitary invariant to classify the Fisher spectrum at maximal entanglement.
result: Maximizers are exchange-symmetric and maximally entangled, with equal sensitivity in all visible directions and at least d^2-1 blind directions; weak compatibility forces at least d^2-1 blind directions for any pure bipartite probe.
conclusion: Fisher sensitivity, weak compatibility, identifiability, and attainable precision are distinct resources; the bipartite obstruction disappears for multipartite probes, where generalized GHZ states can achieve full identifiability.

title: Fermions On A 1d Lattice: Localized Sources And Sinks With Dephasing
authors: Elka Bhattacharya, Sushant Saryal, Soumya Ghosh, Kabir Ramola
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a general one-dimensional spinless fermionic system subject to a localized source, sink, and bulk dephasing. Within the Lindblad framework, we compute the time evolution of the density profile and spatial correlation functions. We find that the presence of bulk dephasing suppresses certain coherent quantum features, such as the Friedel oscillations, and it alters the transport dynamics to exhibit two distinct dynamical regimes instead of three as observed in the absence of dephasing. This effect can be understood as the destruction of ballistic motion caused by the dephasing noise. Under strong dephasing, the density profile becomes similar to the one expected for a classical diffusive regime. We also investigate the system in the presence of both a localized source and sink, placed at a distance of [MATH]. Interestingly, quantum coherence generates secondary density peaks at integer multiples of the source-sink separation [MATH], which are systematically washed out as bulk dephasing drives the system toward the classical diffusive limit.
tldr: This paper studies a 1D fermionic system with localized sources, sinks, and dephasing, showing that dephasing suppresses quantum coherence and drives the system toward classical diffusive transport.
motivation: Understanding the interplay between quantum coherence and dissipation in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and transport.
method: The authors use the Lindblad master equation to model dephasing and compute the time evolution of density profiles and correlation functions for a spinless fermion chain.
result: Bulk dephasing destroys ballistic motion, reduces Friedel oscillations, and leads to two distinct dynamical regimes; under strong dephasing, the system behaves classically diffusive.
conclusion: Dephasing acts as a control parameter that can tune the system from quantum coherent to classical diffusive transport, relevant for quantum thermal machines and information thermodynamics.

title: Dark Polaron Theory For High Intensity Laser Cooling
authors: Marcel Morillas-Rozas, Alberto L\'opez-Garc\'ia, Enamul Haque, Gonzalo Reina Rivero, Javier Cerrillo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.22243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional laser control schemes for cooling and gate operation of trapped ions are limited to the regime of weak laser intensities and small Lamb-Dicke parameters. To overcome this limitation, we present the concept of dark polarons: spatially extended states of pseudospin polarization that are fully decoupled from a lambda laser configuration. In this picture, all high-order Lamb-Dicke terms collapse into a single linear coupling independent of laser intensity. We apply it to definitively elucidate the reasons behind cooling rate limitations observed in recent experimental implementations of electromagnetically induced transparency with high-intensity lasers.
tldr: The paper introduces dark polarons to explain and overcome cooling rate limitations in high-intensity laser cooling of trapped ions.
motivation: Conventional laser cooling schemes for trapped ions are limited to weak laser intensities and small Lamb-Dicke parameters; high-intensity regimes exhibit unexplained cooling rate limitations.
method: The authors develop a dark polaron theory where spatially extended pseudospin states decouple from a lambda laser configuration, collapsing high-order Lamb-Dicke terms into a single linear coupling.
result: The theory elucidates the reasons behind cooling rate limitations observed in EIT experiments with high-intensity lasers.
conclusion: Dark polarons provide a framework to overcome intensity limitations in laser cooling, potentially improving trapped-ion quantum computing and sensing.

title: Entanglement Purification For Arbitrary Multipartite High-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger State
authors: Yu-Qing Kong, Jia-Ye Liu, Hui-Hui Kong, Hai-Rui Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dimensional qudit (i.e., [MATH]-level or [MATH]-state) systems outperform two-dimensional qubit (i.e., 2-level or 2-state) systems in some quantum information processing tasks. We exploit entanglement purification protocols (EPPs) for extracting a subset of high quality arbitrary [MATH]-dimensional [MATH]-partite Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states from a large set of less entangled GHZ states. In our protocols, qudit-flip and phase-flip errors can be corrected, and the fidelity of the output state can be asymptotically improved to unity by iterating the EPP process. Moreover, the schemes are immune to the number of polluted photons, the fidelity thresholds of the proposed EPPs are developed, and the spatial-based single-qudit operations can be well manipulated with a range of balanced beam splitters, and phase shifters. These features make the proposed schemes offer an alternative method for high-dimensional multipartite entanglement purification.
tldr: Proposes entanglement purification protocols for arbitrary multipartite high-dimensional GHZ states, correcting qudit-flip and phase-flip errors.
motivation: High-dimensional qudit systems offer advantages over qubits, but entanglement purification for multipartite high-dimensional GHZ states is needed for practical quantum information processing.
method: Exploits iterative entanglement purification protocols (EPPs) using spatial-based single-qudit operations with balanced beam splitters and phase shifters to correct errors and asymptotically improve fidelity.
result: The protocols can correct qudit-flip and phase-flip errors, achieve unity fidelity asymptotically, and are immune to the number of polluted photons; fidelity thresholds are derived.
conclusion: The proposed EPPs provide an alternative method for high-dimensional multipartite entanglement purification, relevant for quantum networks and quantum information processing.
